2. Objective¶

The objective of this mini-capstone project is to design and implement a Deep Convolutional Generative Adversarial Network (DCGAN) for generating synthetic fashion images using the Fashion-MNIST dataset.

The project aims to:

  • Understand the working principle of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs).
  • Implement a Generator and a Discriminator using deep convolutional neural network architectures.
  • Train the Generator and Discriminator using adversarial learning.
  • Generate new synthetic images that resemble the images in the Fashion-MNIST dataset.
  • Analyze the training behavior of the Generator and Discriminator.
  • Visualize generated images at different stages of training.
  • Evaluate the quality of generated images using visual and quantitative evaluation techniques.
  • Analyze the limitations and performance of the developed DCGAN model.

3. Problem Statement¶

Generative models are an important area of deep learning that can learn the underlying distribution of data and generate new synthetic samples.

In this project, a Deep Convolutional Generative Adversarial Network (DCGAN) is developed to generate synthetic fashion images based on the Fashion-MNIST dataset.

The system consists of two neural networks:

  1. Generator – generates synthetic images from random noise.
  2. Discriminator – distinguishes between real images from the dataset and synthetic images generated by the Generator.

Both networks are trained adversarially so that the Generator gradually learns to produce realistic-looking images that can be difficult for the Discriminator to distinguish from real images.

The project also analyzes the training process and evaluates the quality of generated images using visual and quantitative evaluation methods.

4. Introduction¶

Generative Artificial Intelligence focuses on developing models that can learn patterns and distributions from existing data and generate new data samples.

A Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) is a deep learning framework consisting of two competing neural networks: a Generator and a Discriminator.

The Generator attempts to create realistic synthetic data, while the Discriminator attempts to distinguish real data from generated data. Through this adversarial training process, the Generator gradually improves its ability to generate realistic samples.

GANs have applications in areas such as:

  • Image generation
  • Image-to-image translation
  • Data augmentation
  • Synthetic data generation
  • Image restoration
  • Computer vision
  • Creative content generation
  • Research and simulation

In this project, a Deep Convolutional Generative Adversarial Network (DCGAN) is implemented for synthetic fashion image generation using the Fashion-MNIST dataset.

The project goes beyond basic GAN implementation by analyzing training losses, generated-image progression, visual quality, and quantitative evaluation.

5. Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) Concept¶

A Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) consists of two neural networks:

5.1 Generator¶

The Generator creates synthetic data from a random noise vector.

The Generator receives random noise as input and transforms it into a synthetic image.

Random Noise
     ↓
 Generator
     ↓
Synthetic Image

5.2 Discriminator

The Discriminator receives both real and generated images and attempts to determine whether an image is real or generated.

        Real Image ─────────┐
                          ↓
                    Discriminator
                          ↓
                    Real / Fake
                          ↑
        Generated Image ────┘

5.3 Adversarial Training

The Generator and Discriminator have competing objectives.

The Generator attempts to generate images that appear real. The Discriminator attempts to correctly identify real and generated images.

During training, both networks are updated repeatedly. The Generator learns from the feedback provided by the Discriminator and gradually improves the quality of generated images.

Basic GAN Process

             Random Noise
                  │
                  ▼
            ┌───────────┐
            │ Generator │
            └─────┬─────┘
                  │
                  ▼
             Fake Image
                  │
                  ▼
            ┌──────────────┐
            │Discriminator │
            └──────┬───────┘
                   │
          ┌────────┴────────┐
          ▼                 ▼
      Real Image        Fake Image
          │                 │
          └────────┬────────┘
                   ▼
              Real / Fake
                Output

## 6. Why DCGAN?

A basic GAN can use fully connected neural networks, but image data
contains important spatial information. Convolutional neural networks
are well suited for learning spatial patterns and visual features.

A Deep Convolutional Generative Adversarial Network (DCGAN) combines
GAN-based adversarial learning with convolutional neural network
architectures.

In this project, DCGAN is selected because:

- It is specifically designed for image generation tasks.
- Convolutional layers can learn spatial features from images.
- The Generator can use transposed convolutional layers to progressively
  construct images.
- The Discriminator can use convolutional layers to identify visual
  patterns.
- It provides a suitable architecture for generating Fashion-MNIST
  images.
- It allows us to analyze both image quality and adversarial training
  behavior.

### DCGAN Conceptual Architecture

```text
                    Random Noise
                         │
                         ▼
                 ┌──────────────┐
                 │   Generator  │
                 │  DCNN-based  │
                 └──────┬───────┘
                        │
                        ▼
                  Generated Image
                        │
                        ▼
                 ┌──────────────┐
                 │ Discriminator│
                 │  CNN-based   │
                 └──────┬───────┘
                        │
                        ▼
                   Real / Fake

## 8. Dataset Description

### Dataset Name

**Fashion-MNIST**

Fashion-MNIST is an image dataset containing grayscale images of
fashion-related items. It is commonly used for machine learning and
deep learning experiments involving image data.

### Dataset Characteristics

- Image type: Grayscale
- Image size: 28 × 28 pixels
- Number of classes: 10
- Each image represents a fashion item.
- The dataset can be used directly through TensorFlow/Keras dataset
  utilities.

### Fashion Categories

The dataset contains the following categories:

1. T-shirt / Top
2. Trouser
3. Pullover
4. Dress
5. Coat
6. Sandal
7. Shirt
8. Sneaker
9. Bag
10. Ankle Boot

### Role of the Dataset in This Project

In this project, the Fashion-MNIST images are used as real training
samples for the Discriminator.

The Generator does not directly receive real images as input.
Instead, it receives random noise and attempts to generate synthetic
fashion images.

The Discriminator receives:

- Real Fashion-MNIST images
- Generated images from the Generator

and learns to distinguish between the two.

13. Data Preprocessing¶

The original Fashion-MNIST images contain pixel values in the range 0 to 255.

For stable GAN training, the images are converted to floating-point values and normalized to the range [-1, 1].

The output activation of the Generator will use tanh, which also produces values in the range [-1, 1]. Therefore, both real and generated images will use the same numerical range during adversarial training.

In [10]:
# ============================================================
# Normalize image pixel values from [0, 255] to [-1, 1]
# ============================================================

X_train = X_train.astype("float32")

X_train = (X_train - 127.5) / 127.5

print("Minimum pixel value after normalization:", X_train.min())
print("Maximum pixel value after normalization:", X_train.max())

Maximum pixel value after normalization: 1.0

15. Define Generator¶

The Generator is responsible for creating synthetic fashion images from a random noise vector.

The model starts with a low-dimensional random noise vector and progressively transforms it into a 28 × 28 grayscale image using dense and transposed convolutional layers.

Batch normalization is used to improve training stability, while ReLU activation functions are used in the intermediate layers. The final layer uses the tanh activation function because the training images were normalized to the range [-1, 1].

In [13]:
# ============================================================
# Section 15: Define Generator
# ============================================================

# Dimension of the random noise vector given to the Generator
LATENT_DIM = 100

print("Latent dimension:", LATENT_DIM)

Latent dimension: 100
In [14]:
# ============================================================
# Build the DCGAN Generator
# ============================================================

def build_generator():
    """
    Creates the Generator network.

    Input:
        Random noise vector of size LATENT_DIM.

    Output:
        Generated grayscale image of shape 28 x 28 x 1.
    """

    model = keras.Sequential(name="DCGAN_Generator")

    # Start with a random noise vector
    model.add(
        layers.Input(shape=(LATENT_DIM,))
    )

    # Project the noise vector into a small spatial feature map
    model.add(
        layers.Dense(7 * 7 * 128, use_bias=False)
    )
    model.add(
        layers.BatchNormalization()
    )
    model.add(
        layers.ReLU()
    )

    # Reshape into a 7 x 7 feature map with 128 channels
    model.add(
        layers.Reshape((7, 7, 128))
    )

    # Upsample: 7 x 7 -> 14 x 14
    model.add(
        layers.Conv2DTranspose(
            64,
            kernel_size=5,
            strides=2,
            padding="same",
            use_bias=False
        )
    )
    model.add(
        layers.BatchNormalization()
    )
    model.add(
        layers.ReLU()
    )

    # Upsample: 14 x 14 -> 28 x 28
    model.add(
        layers.Conv2DTranspose(
            32,
            kernel_size=5,
            strides=2,
            padding="same",
            use_bias=False
        )
    )
    model.add(
        layers.BatchNormalization()
    )
    model.add(
        layers.ReLU()
    )

    # Final layer produces a single-channel grayscale image
    model.add(
        layers.Conv2DTranspose(
            1,
            kernel_size=5,
            strides=1,
            padding="same",
            activation="tanh"
        )
    )

    return model


# Create the Generator
generator = build_generator()

print("Generator created successfully.")

Generator created successfully.

16. Generator Architecture Analysis¶

The Generator transforms a 100-dimensional random noise vector into a 28 × 28 × 1 grayscale image.

The architecture progressively increases the spatial dimensions:

  • Dense layer: Projects the latent vector into a feature representation.
  • Reshape layer: Converts the feature vector into a 7 × 7 feature map.
  • First Conv2DTranspose: Upsamples 7 × 7 to 14 × 14.
  • Second Conv2DTranspose: Upsamples 14 × 14 to 28 × 28.
  • Final Conv2DTranspose: Produces a single-channel grayscale image.
  • Batch Normalization: Helps stabilize the training process.
  • ReLU: Provides nonlinear transformation in intermediate layers.
  • Tanh: Produces output values in the range [-1, 1], matching the normalized training images.

17. Define Discriminator¶

The Discriminator is a convolutional neural network that receives a 28 × 28 grayscale image and predicts whether the image is a real sample from the Fashion-MNIST dataset or a synthetic image produced by the Generator.

The Discriminator uses convolutional layers to extract spatial features from the images.

Unlike the Generator, the Discriminator reduces the spatial dimensions while increasing the number of learned feature channels.

The final output is a single value representing the probability that the input image is real.

In [19]:
# ============================================================
# Section 17: Build the DCGAN Discriminator
# ============================================================

def build_discriminator():
    """
    Creates the Discriminator network.

    Input:
        28 x 28 x 1 grayscale image

    Output:
        Single probability indicating real or fake.
    """

    model = keras.Sequential(name="DCGAN_Discriminator")

    # Input image: 28 x 28 x 1
    model.add(
        layers.Input(shape=(28, 28, 1))
    )

    # Extract low-level visual features
    model.add(
        layers.Conv2D(
            64,
            kernel_size=5,
            strides=2,
            padding="same"
        )
    )
    model.add(
        layers.LeakyReLU(negative_slope=0.2)
    )
    model.add(
        layers.Dropout(0.3)
    )

    # Extract deeper visual features
    model.add(
        layers.Conv2D(
            128,
            kernel_size=5,
            strides=2,
            padding="same"
        )
    )
    model.add(
        layers.LeakyReLU(negative_slope=0.2)
    )
    model.add(
        layers.Dropout(0.3)
    )

    # Convert feature maps into a single prediction
    model.add(
        layers.Flatten()
    )

    model.add(
        layers.Dense(1)
    )

    return model


# Create the Discriminator
discriminator = build_discriminator()

print("Discriminator created successfully.")

Discriminator created successfully.

20. Define Loss Functions¶

The DCGAN uses two separate loss functions:

Discriminator Loss¶

The Discriminator learns to classify:

  • Real images as real.
  • Generated images as fake.

Its loss is calculated using the predictions for both real and generated images.

Generator Loss¶

The Generator attempts to produce images that the Discriminator classifies as real.

Therefore, the Generator is trained using the Discriminator's prediction on generated images.

Binary Cross-Entropy is used to calculate both losses.

The adversarial training objective can be summarized as:

Generator:
Random Noise → Generated Image → Discriminator → Generator Loss

Discriminator:
Real Image → Discriminator → Real Loss
Fake Image → Discriminator → Fake Loss
                         ↓
                 Discriminator Loss
In [22]:
# ============================================================
# Section 20: Define GAN Loss Functions
# ============================================================

# Binary Cross-Entropy is commonly used for GAN adversarial loss
cross_entropy = keras.losses.BinaryCrossentropy(from_logits=True)


def discriminator_loss(real_output, fake_output):
    """
    Calculate the total Discriminator loss.

    Real images should be classified as 1.
    Generated images should be classified as 0.
    """

    real_loss = cross_entropy(
        tf.ones_like(real_output),
        real_output
    )

    fake_loss = cross_entropy(
        tf.zeros_like(fake_output),
        fake_output
    )

    total_loss = real_loss + fake_loss

    return total_loss


def generator_loss(fake_output):
    """
    Calculate the Generator loss.

    The Generator wants the Discriminator to classify
    generated images as real (label = 1).
    """

    loss = cross_entropy(
        tf.ones_like(fake_output),
        fake_output
    )

    return loss


print("GAN loss functions defined successfully.")

GAN loss functions defined successfully.

21. Define Optimizers¶

The Generator and Discriminator use separate Adam optimizers.

Adam is selected because it provides adaptive learning rates and is commonly used for training neural networks.

Separate optimizers are required because the Generator and Discriminator have different trainable parameters and different optimization objectives.

In [23]:
# ============================================================
# Section 21: Define Optimizers
# ============================================================

# Learning rate used for both networks
LEARNING_RATE = 0.0002

# Adam optimizer for the Generator
generator_optimizer = keras.optimizers.Adam(
    learning_rate=LEARNING_RATE,
    beta_1=0.5
)

# Adam optimizer for the Discriminator
discriminator_optimizer = keras.optimizers.Adam(
    learning_rate=LEARNING_RATE,
    beta_1=0.5
)

print("Optimizers created successfully.")
print("Learning rate:", LEARNING_RATE)
print("Adam beta_1:", 0.5)

Optimizers created successfully.
Learning rate: 0.0002
Adam beta_1: 0.5

Random Noise ↓ Generator ↓ Fake Images ↓ Discriminator ↓ Calculate Loss ↓ Calculate Gradients ↓ Update Generator + Discriminator

22. Define Training Step¶

A single training step performs one adversarial update of the Generator and Discriminator.

The process is:

  1. Generate random noise.
  2. Generate synthetic images using the Generator.
  3. Pass real images through the Discriminator.
  4. Pass generated images through the Discriminator.
  5. Calculate Generator and Discriminator losses.
  6. Calculate gradients using automatic differentiation.
  7. Update the Generator parameters.
  8. Update the Discriminator parameters.

The tf.GradientTape mechanism is used to calculate gradients for both networks.

In [24]:
# ============================================================
# Section 22: Define One GAN Training Step
# ============================================================

@tf.function
def train_step(real_images):
    """
    Performs one adversarial training step.

    Parameters:
        real_images: A batch of real Fashion-MNIST images.

    Returns:
        Generator loss and Discriminator loss.
    """

    # Get the number of images in the current batch
    batch_size = tf.shape(real_images)[0]

    # Generate random latent vectors
    noise = tf.random.normal(
        shape=(batch_size, LATENT_DIM)
    )

    # Record operations needed for gradient calculation
    with tf.GradientTape() as gen_tape, tf.GradientTape() as disc_tape:

        # Generate fake images
        generated_images = generator(
            noise,
            training=True
        )

        # Discriminator predictions
        real_output = discriminator(
            real_images,
            training=True
        )

        fake_output = discriminator(
            generated_images,
            training=True
        )

        # Calculate both losses
        gen_loss = generator_loss(fake_output)

        disc_loss = discriminator_loss(
            real_output,
            fake_output
        )

    # Calculate gradients for the Generator
    gradients_of_generator = gen_tape.gradient(
        gen_loss,
        generator.trainable_variables
    )

    # Calculate gradients for the Discriminator
    gradients_of_discriminator = disc_tape.gradient(
        disc_loss,
        discriminator.trainable_variables
    )

    # Update Generator parameters
    generator_optimizer.apply_gradients(
        zip(
            gradients_of_generator,
            generator.trainable_variables
        )
    )

    # Update Discriminator parameters
    discriminator_optimizer.apply_gradients(
        zip(
            gradients_of_discriminator,
            discriminator.trainable_variables
        )
    )

    return gen_loss, disc_loss

# Generate images from the fixed noise vectors

def generate_and_plot_images(model, noise, title="Generated Images"):
    """
    Generate and display images from a fixed set of latent vectors.
    """

    predictions = model(
        noise,
        training=False
    )

    plt.figure(figsize=(8, 8))

    for i in range(predictions.shape[0]):
        plt.subplot(4, 4, i + 1)

        # Convert pixel values from [-1, 1] to [0, 1]
        image = (predictions[i, :, :, 0] + 1) / 2

        plt.imshow(image, cmap="gray")
        plt.axis("off")

    plt.suptitle(title)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

24. DCGAN Training¶

The DCGAN is trained using an adversarial training process.

For each batch:

  1. A batch of real Fashion-MNIST images is selected.
  2. Random noise vectors are generated.
  3. The Generator creates synthetic images.
  4. The Discriminator evaluates both real and synthetic images.
  5. Generator and Discriminator losses are calculated.
  6. Gradients are calculated using backpropagation.
  7. Both networks are updated using their respective optimizers.

The process is repeated for multiple epochs so that the Generator gradually learns to generate images that resemble the Fashion-MNIST training distribution.

A fixed noise vector is used periodically to visualize the Generator's progress throughout training.

In [29]:
# ============================================================
# Section 24: DCGAN Training Configuration
# ============================================================

# Number of epochs for the initial training experiment
EPOCHS = 20

# Number of examples saved for progress visualization
SAVE_INTERVAL = 5

# Lists used to store training losses
generator_losses = []
discriminator_losses = []

# Create folders for generated images and results
os.makedirs("generated_images", exist_ok=True)
os.makedirs("results", exist_ok=True)

print("Training configuration ready.")
print("Epochs:", EPOCHS)
print("Image save interval:", SAVE_INTERVAL)

Training configuration ready.
Epochs: 20
Image save interval: 5
In [30]:
# ============================================================
# Function to save generated images during training
# ============================================================

def save_generated_images(model, noise, epoch):
    """
    Generate images using fixed noise and save them to disk.
    """

    predictions = model(
        noise,
        training=False
    )

    plt.figure(figsize=(8, 8))

    for i in range(16):
        plt.subplot(4, 4, i + 1)

        # Convert [-1, 1] back to [0, 1]
        image = (predictions[i, :, :, 0] + 1) / 2

        plt.imshow(image, cmap="gray")
        plt.axis("off")

    plt.suptitle(f"DCGAN Generated Images - Epoch {epoch}")

    plt.tight_layout()

    # Save the generated image grid
    filename = f"generated_images/epoch_{epoch:03d}.png"
    plt.savefig(filename, dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")

    plt.show()
    plt.close()

    print(f"Saved: {filename}")
In [31]:
# ============================================================
# DCGAN Training Loop
# ============================================================

print("Starting DCGAN training...\n")

for epoch in range(1, EPOCHS + 1):

    # Store losses for the current epoch
    epoch_generator_loss = []
    epoch_discriminator_loss = []

    # Train using every batch in the dataset
    for real_images in train_dataset:

        # Perform one adversarial training step
        gen_loss, disc_loss = train_step(real_images)

        # Store the loss values
        epoch_generator_loss.append(float(gen_loss))
        epoch_discriminator_loss.append(float(disc_loss))

    # Calculate average loss for the epoch
    avg_gen_loss = np.mean(epoch_generator_loss)
    avg_disc_loss = np.mean(epoch_discriminator_loss)

    # Store the average losses
    generator_losses.append(avg_gen_loss)
    discriminator_losses.append(avg_disc_loss)

    # Display epoch results
    print(
        f"Epoch {epoch:03d}/{EPOCHS} | "
        f"Generator Loss: {avg_gen_loss:.4f} | "
        f"Discriminator Loss: {avg_disc_loss:.4f}"
    )

    # Save generated images at selected intervals
    if epoch == 1 or epoch % SAVE_INTERVAL == 0:
        save_generated_images(
            generator,
            fixed_noise,
            epoch
        )

print("\nDCGAN training completed successfully.")

25. Save the Trained Models¶

After completing the initial training, the trained Generator and Discriminator are saved so that the learned model parameters can be reused later without retraining the complete GAN.

The Generator can be used independently to generate new synthetic Fashion-MNIST-style images.

In [32]:

# ============================================================

os.makedirs("models/discriminator", exist_ok=True)

# Save the trained Generator
generator.save("models/generator/dcgan_generator.keras")

# Save the trained Discriminator
discriminator.save("models/discriminator/dcgan_discriminator.keras")

27. Generator Loss Analysis¶

The Generator loss represents how effectively the Generator is attempting to produce images that the Discriminator classifies as real.

The Generator loss is recorded after each training epoch.

Plotting this loss allows us to observe how the Generator's optimization behavior changes during training.

In [35]:
# ============================================================
# Section 27: Generator Loss Analysis
# ============================================================

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 5))

plt.plot(
    range(1, len(generator_losses) + 1),
    generator_losses,
    label="Generator Loss"
)

plt.xlabel("Epoch")
plt.ylabel("Loss")
plt.title("Generator Loss During DCGAN Training")
plt.legend()
plt.grid(True)

plt.show()

28. Discriminator Loss Analysis¶

The Discriminator loss measures the ability of the Discriminator to distinguish real Fashion-MNIST images from images generated by the Generator.

The loss is calculated using both real and generated samples.

The Discriminator loss is analyzed together with the Generator loss because GAN training involves competition between the two networks.

In [36]:
# ============================================================
# Section 28: Discriminator Loss Analysis
# ============================================================

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 5))

plt.plot(
    range(1, len(discriminator_losses) + 1),
    discriminator_losses,
    label="Discriminator Loss"
)

plt.xlabel("Epoch")
plt.ylabel("Loss")
plt.title("Discriminator Loss During DCGAN Training")
plt.legend()
plt.grid(True)

plt.show()

29. Combined Generator and Discriminator Loss Analysis¶

The Generator and Discriminator losses are plotted together to observe their adversarial training behavior.

GAN losses should not be interpreted in the same way as conventional classification accuracy. The two networks are competing against each other, so their losses can fluctuate as the adversarial training progresses.

Therefore, the loss curves are analyzed together with the generated images rather than using loss values alone to determine image quality.

In [37]:
# ============================================================
# Section 29: Combined Loss Analysis
# ============================================================

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 5))

epochs_range = range(1, len(generator_losses) + 1)

plt.plot(
    epochs_range,
    generator_losses,
    label="Generator Loss"
)

plt.plot(
    epochs_range,
    discriminator_losses,
    label="Discriminator Loss"
)

plt.xlabel("Epoch")
plt.ylabel("Loss")
plt.title("Generator vs Discriminator Loss")
plt.legend()
plt.grid(True)

plt.show()

31. Real vs Generated Image Comparison¶

The quality of the trained Generator is visually examined by comparing real Fashion-MNIST images with synthetic images generated by the DCGAN.

Real images are taken directly from the dataset, while generated images are produced from previously unseen random latent vectors.

This comparison provides a qualitative evaluation of whether the Generator has learned meaningful visual patterns from the training data.

In [39]:
# ============================================================
# Section 31: Real vs Generated Image Comparison
# ============================================================

# Select 10 real images
real_images = X_train[:10]

# Generate 10 synthetic images
comparison_noise = tf.random.normal(
    shape=(10, LATENT_DIM),
    seed=SEED + 2
)

generated_images = generator(
    comparison_noise,
    training=False
)

plt.figure(figsize=(12, 5))

# -------------------------
# Real images
# -------------------------
for i in range(10):
    plt.subplot(2, 10, i + 1)

    plt.imshow(
        real_images[i, :, :, 0],
        cmap="gray"
    )

    plt.axis("off")

    if i == 0:
        plt.ylabel("Real", fontsize=12)

# -------------------------
# Generated images
# -------------------------

34. Advanced Evaluation Preparation¶

Advanced evaluation attempts to measure generated image quality using feature representations rather than relying only on visual inspection or GAN training losses.

Because Fashion-MNIST contains 28 × 28 grayscale images, this project uses a domain-specific feature extractor trained on Fashion-MNIST.

The feature extractor learns a 128-dimensional representation of the images. These feature representations are later used to compare real and generated images quantitatively.

The evaluation results are interpreted together with visual inspection and training-loss curves.

35. Create Evaluation Dataset¶

A separate evaluation set is prepared to compare the statistical characteristics of real Fashion-MNIST images and generated images.

The evaluation uses equal numbers of real and generated samples.

The real images represent the reference data distribution, while the generated images represent the distribution learned by the DCGAN.

In [42]:
# ============================================================
# Section 35: Create Evaluation Dataset
# ============================================================

# Number of images used for quantitative evaluation
EVAL_SAMPLES = 10000

# Use a fixed number of real Fashion-MNIST images
real_eval_images = X_train[:EVAL_SAMPLES]

# Generate the same number of synthetic images
evaluation_noise = tf.random.normal(
    shape=(EVAL_SAMPLES, LATENT_DIM),
    seed=SEED + 10
)

generated_eval_images = generator(
    evaluation_noise,
    training=False
)

print("Real evaluation images:", real_eval_images.shape)
print("Generated evaluation images:", generated_eval_images.shape)

Real evaluation images: (10000, 28, 28, 1)
Generated evaluation images: (10000, 28, 28, 1)

36. Build Fashion-MNIST Feature Extractor¶

A CNN-based feature extractor is trained on Fashion-MNIST classification.

The intermediate feature representation learned by this network is used for quantitative comparison between real and generated images.

This provides a domain-specific feature space because the extractor has learned visual characteristics directly from Fashion-MNIST.

The feature extractor is not part of the GAN itself. It is used only for post-training evaluation.

In [43]:
# ============================================================
# Section 36: Build Feature Extractor
# ============================================================

def build_feature_extractor():
    """
    CNN used to learn Fashion-MNIST feature representations.
    """

    inputs = keras.Input(shape=(28, 28, 1))

    # First convolutional block
    x = layers.Conv2D(
        32,
        kernel_size=3,
        activation="relu",
        padding="same"
    )(inputs)

    x = layers.MaxPooling2D()(x)

    # Second convolutional block
    x = layers.Conv2D(
        64,
        kernel_size=3,
        activation="relu",
        padding="same"
    )(x)

    x = layers.MaxPooling2D()(x)

    # Third convolutional block
    x = layers.Conv2D(
        128,
        kernel_size=3,
        activation="relu",
        padding="same"
    )(x)

    x = layers.GlobalAveragePooling2D()(x)

    # Compact feature representation
    features = layers.Dense(
        128,
        activation="relu",
        name="feature_vector"
    )(x)

    outputs = layers.Dense(
        10,
        activation="softmax"
    )(features)

    model = keras.Model(
        inputs,
        outputs,
        name="FashionMNIST_Feature_Extractor"
    )

    feature_model = keras.Model(
        inputs,
        features,
        name="FashionMNIST_Feature_Model"
    )

    return model, feature_model


feature_classifier, feature_extractor = build_feature_extractor()

feature_classifier.summary()

39. Domain-Specific Fréchet Distance¶

The Fréchet distance is calculated between the feature distributions of real and generated Fashion-MNIST images.

The calculation uses:

  • Mean feature vector of real images
  • Covariance matrix of real features
  • Mean feature vector of generated images
  • Covariance matrix of generated features

A smaller distance indicates that the generated feature distribution is closer to the real-image feature distribution.

This project uses a Fashion-MNIST-trained feature extractor rather than the standard ImageNet Inception feature extractor. Therefore, the value is reported as a domain-specific FID-style metric and should not be directly compared with standard Inception-FID values from other studies.

In [46]:
# ============================================================
# Section 39: Calculate Domain-Specific Fréchet Distance
# ============================================================

from scipy.linalg import sqrtm


def calculate_frechet_distance(real_features, generated_features):
    """
    Calculate the Fréchet distance between two feature distributions.
    """

    # Calculate feature means
    mu_real = np.mean(
        real_features,
        axis=0
    )

    mu_generated = np.mean(
        generated_features,
        axis=0
    )

    # Calculate covariance matrices
    sigma_real = np.cov(
        real_features,
        rowvar=False
    )

    sigma_generated = np.cov(
        generated_features,
        rowvar=False
    )

    # Difference between means
    mean_difference = mu_real - mu_generated

    # Product of covariance matrices
    covariance_product = (
        sigma_real @ sigma_generated
    )

    # Numerical stability
    covariance_sqrt = sqrtm(
        covariance_product
    )

    # Handle small numerical imaginary components
    if np.iscomplexobj(covariance_sqrt):
        covariance_sqrt = covariance_sqrt.real

    # Fréchet distance
    distance = (
        mean_difference @ mean_difference
        + np.trace(sigma_real)
        + np.trace(sigma_generated)
        - 2 * np.trace(covariance_sqrt)
    )

    return float(distance)


domain_fid = calculate_frechet_distance(
    real_features,
    generated_features
)

print("=" * 60)
print("DOMAIN-SPECIFIC FID-STYLE EVALUATION")
print("=" * 60)
print(f"Fréchet Feature Distance: {domain_fid:.4f}")

40. Generated Image Diversity Analysis¶

Visual quality alone does not determine the quality of a generative model.

A Generator may produce visually plausible images while generating highly similar samples.

Therefore, sample diversity is examined by measuring the variation between generated feature representations.

Higher feature variation indicates greater diversity among the generated samples, although diversity should always be interpreted together with image quality.

In [47]:
# ============================================================
# Section 40: Diversity Analysis
# ============================================================

# Calculate standard deviation for each feature dimension
feature_std = np.std(
    generated_features,
    axis=0
)

# Average feature variation
average_feature_std = np.mean(
    feature_std
)

print("=" * 60)
print("GENERATED IMAGE DIVERSITY")
print("=" * 60)
print(
    f"Average feature standard deviation: "
    f"{average_feature_std:.6f}"
)

41. Nearest-Neighbor Analysis¶

Nearest-neighbor analysis compares generated samples with real Fashion-MNIST samples in the learned feature space.

This provides an additional qualitative check for similarity between generated and real samples.

Very close nearest neighbors do not automatically indicate memorization, but the analysis helps investigate whether generated samples contain substantial variation rather than being identical copies.

In [48]:
# ============================================================
# Section 41: Nearest-Neighbor Analysis
# ============================================================

from sklearn.metrics import pairwise_distances

# Use a manageable subset for nearest-neighbor analysis
NN_SAMPLES = 1000

real_nn_features = real_features[:NN_SAMPLES]
generated_nn_features = generated_features[:NN_SAMPLES]

# Calculate pairwise distances
distances = pairwise_distances(
    generated_nn_features,
    real_nn_features,
    metric="euclidean"
)

# Find closest real sample for every generated sample
nearest_distances = np.min(
    distances,
    axis=1
)

print("=" * 60)
print("NEAREST-NEIGHBOR ANALYSIS")
print("=" * 60)

print(
    "Mean nearest-neighbor distance:",
    nearest_distances.mean()
)

print(
    "Minimum nearest-neighbor distance:",
    nearest_distances.min()
)

print(
    "Maximum nearest-neighbor distance:",
    nearest_distances.max()
)

47. Final Model Evaluation Summary¶

The DCGAN was evaluated using multiple complementary approaches:

  1. Training Loss Analysis

    • Generator loss
    • Discriminator loss
    • Combined loss curves

  2. Visual Evaluation

    • Generated image samples
    • Real versus generated comparison
    • Training progression

  3. Feature-Based Evaluation

    • Domain-specific Fréchet feature distance
    • Real and generated feature distributions

  4. Diversity Analysis

    • Feature standard deviation
    • Variation among generated samples

  5. Nearest-Neighbor Analysis

    • Mean nearest-neighbor distance
    • Minimum nearest-neighbor distance
    • Maximum nearest-neighbor distance

No single metric is used as the only measure of GAN quality. The results are interpreted collectively because GAN losses, visual quality, distribution similarity, and sample diversity measure different aspects of generative performance.

48. Applications of GANs¶

Generative Adversarial Networks can be used in several applications where synthetic data or realistic generated content is required.

Examples include:

  • Synthetic image generation
  • Data augmentation
  • Image-to-image translation
  • Computer vision research
  • Fashion and product design
  • Medical image research
  • Creative content generation
  • Privacy-preserving synthetic data generation

In this project, the DCGAN is specifically used to generate synthetic Fashion-MNIST-style grayscale images.

49. Limitations¶

The implemented DCGAN has several limitations:

  1. GAN training can be unstable because the Generator and Discriminator must learn simultaneously.

  2. Generated image quality depends strongly on the architecture, hyperparameters, dataset, and number of training epochs.

  3. Mode collapse can occur when the Generator produces similar samples instead of representing the full data distribution.

  4. Fashion-MNIST contains relatively simple 28 × 28 grayscale images, so the results do not represent the challenges of high-resolution image generation.

  5. The domain-specific Fréchet feature distance used in this project depends on the quality of the Fashion-MNIST feature extractor.

  6. Quantitative metrics cannot completely replace human visual inspection of generated samples.

50. Future Scope¶

The project can be extended in several directions:

  • Train the DCGAN for more epochs.
  • Experiment with different Generator and Discriminator architectures.
  • Tune learning rate, batch size, latent dimension, and optimizer parameters.
  • Investigate techniques for reducing mode collapse.
  • Compare DCGAN with other GAN architectures.
  • Use conditional GANs to generate specific Fashion-MNIST categories.
  • Use higher-resolution datasets for more challenging image generation.
  • Explore additional feature-based evaluation methods.
  • Compare generated samples across multiple training configurations.
  • Investigate more advanced generative models such as StyleGAN and diffusion-based approaches.

51. Conclusion¶

In this project, a Deep Convolutional Generative Adversarial Network (DCGAN) was implemented using the Fashion-MNIST dataset.

The Generator learned to transform random latent vectors into synthetic 28 × 28 grayscale images, while the Discriminator learned to distinguish between real Fashion-MNIST images and generated samples.

The project included complete model training, generated-image visualization, Generator and Discriminator loss analysis, real-versus- generated comparison, feature-based evaluation, diversity analysis, and nearest-neighbor analysis.

The results demonstrate how adversarial training can be used to learn visual patterns from a dataset and generate new synthetic samples.

The evaluation was performed using multiple complementary approaches rather than relying on a single metric. This provides a broader view of the model's training behavior, generated image quality, feature similarity, and sample diversity.
